title: Pick Up the Shovel
author: John McLean
summary: John McLean, writing as Wisdom From Dad, uses his own string of childhood and young-adult jobs to make a point about diligence. He worked for cereal, for a hamburger and Coke, and for a paycheck, but the job that mattered most was a financial analyst role he did not enjoy and had to work hard to master. His tenet is that working hard is about effort, while working diligently is effort applied consistently toward something that matters, because the work also forms the person you become. He retells Stephen Covey's story of giving his son the objective "keep the lawn green and clean" so the boy would own a result rather than follow instructions. For fathers, the application is to model household work, let children own a task, ask questions instead of rescuing them, and recognise effort and persistence. The practice for the week is to give a child a small, tangible job and resist the urge to take over.
points: Diligence is effort applied consistently toward something that matters, and the work done today also produces the person you become.
Covey's "green and clean" lawn shows that children learn responsibility when given ownership of a result, not a list of instructions.
Children watch what fathers do, so they need to see their dad doing the work that keeps the home running and finishing what he starts.
When a child hits a problem, a father should ask a question such as "What could you try?" rather than hand over the answer.
The goal of a child's task is not a perfect result but the experience of discovering "I can figure things out," and recognising effort turns diligence into a habit.
quotes: There’s a difference between working hard and working diligently. Working hard is about effort. Working diligently is about effort applied consistently toward something that matters.

Diligence is the willingness to keep doing the right work, even when the payoff isn’t immediate, because the work you do today isn’t just producing today’s result; it’s also producing the person you become in the process.
Covey wasn’t teaching his son how to mow a lawn. He was teaching him how to take responsibility for a result.
But if we’re always telling our kids exactly what to do, when to do it and how to do it, we can accidentally teach them that responsibility means following instructions.
And it’s not enough that they see you leave for the office. Your kids need to see you doing things around the house.
The important part is to let them own the work. Don’t hover. Don’t take over.
Because the greatest gift we can give our kids isn’t a life without difficult work. It’s the confidence to believe they can do difficult things.
